name: Dendi (Benin)
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dendi (Benin) is not in the catalog. All eight keyword-matched Glottolog items (Bergmann x2, Bundgaard-Nielsen et al., Baker, Albert, Choi et al., Sharf/Scharf x2) are Glottolog tagging artefacts — 'stops' in the title — about German, Wubuy, Korean, Hebrew and English; none concerns Dendi (priority none).org APIs, the Google Books GData feed (snippet text) and the Wayback Machine. The real Dendi literature is: Tersis 1968 (Bulletin de la SELAF 10, Niger Dendi; BnF record corrects the earlier audit's title; snippet 'le dendi est une langue à tons'; print only, high priority), Nicolaï 1978 'Les parlers dendi' (ALLA 4: 47-79; snippet: tone system 'tout à fait comparable au système zarma' and unlike Djenné/Tombouctou/Gao; tones high/low/rising; T&F reprint paywalled), Nicolaï 1981 (SELAF, print), Zima 1994 lexicon with phonological sketch (print), Dramane 1993 mémoire (not findable), Zima 1976 and Nicolaï & Zima 1997 (print). The one open first-hand statement obtained and read is Nicolaï 1982, Studies in African Linguistics 13(3): 273-322 (fetched sources as a Wayback copy of the open FLVC full-issue PDF, saved with page images): p. 281 classes Dendi with Zarma as 'Type 4', a four-tone syllabic system (reducible to H/L on moras), against the fixed/free stress-accent systems of Western, Eastern and Northern Songhay; fn. 12 notes Tersis's three-tone analysis of Gaya Dendi. Salmons 2003 p. 34 (secondary, snippet) and a 1986 JALL review (snippet) repeat this four-tone classification; CENALA 1990 (open PDF) shows Dendi written with tone diacritics but gives no count. Coding implication: tone language, no lexical word stress; Wikipedia's 'four-tone language' line traces to Salmons citing Nicolaï. Everything fetched sources is under with.

new_statements.quote: Type 4 : Système tonal permettant quatre distinctions dans le cadre syllabique {CV́, CV̀, CV̌, CV̂}. Il peut dans la plupart des cas se réduire à une opposition entre deux valeurs tonales par le biais d'une analyse en mores (56). Les combinaisons des tons à l'intérieur des polysyllabes sont déterminées par des règles, de même que les combinaisons des unités entre elles. Ce système est réalisé en zarma et en dendi (57) qui ne se distinguent l'un de l'autre que par l'existence en zarma de quelques règles portant sur les contrastes dans le cadre des unités en combinaison (58). [fn. 57:] Toutefois, N. TERSIS dit que le dendi de Gaya a trois tons, cf. N. TERSIS 'Le dendi' ouvr. cit. p. 3-4.
new_statements.translation: Type 4: A tonal system allowing four distinctions within the syllable frame {CV́ (high), CV̀ (low), CV̌ (rising), CV̂ (falling)}. In most cases it can be reduced to an opposition between two tonal values by means of a mora analysis. The combinations of tones inside polysyllables are determined by rules, as are the combinations of units with one another. This system is realized in Zarma and in Dendi, which differ from each other only by the existence in Zarma of a few rules bearing on contrasts within units in combination. [fn. 57:] However, N. Tersis says that the Dendi of Gaya has three tones, cf. N. Tersis, 'Le dendi', pp. 3-4.
new_statements.citation: Nicolaï, Robert. 1979. Les dialectes du songhay (contribution à l'étude des changements linguistiques). Thèse d'État, Université de Nice; published unchanged as Bibliothèque de la SELAF 85-86, Paris: SELAF, 1981. §1.3.4 'Aperçu statique des systèmes prosodiques', pp. 47-49 (quote p. 48 and fn. 57). Identical wording in Nicolaï 1982, Studies in African Linguistics 13(3): 281 and fn. 12.
new_statements.locator: Thesis p. 48 (PDF p. 57), §1.3.4, 'Type 4', with fn. 57; = SAL 13(3), 1982, p. 281 with fn. 12. Auxiliary-accent remarks: thesis pp. 288-290 (PDF 294-296) = SAL pp. 279-280; tone inventory for Zarma/Dendi: thesis p. 291 = SAL p. 282 §5.
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dendi (Benin: Djougou, Parakou, Kandi) has no word-stress system: it is a lexical tone language with four syllable-level tonal distinctions (high, low, rising, falling), the contour tones being decomposable as sequences of H and L on moras and restricted to final or long syllables; tone patterns of polysyllables are rule-governed. Accent (intensity) exists in Songhay only as a distinctive system in the Western, Eastern and Northern dialects; in the tonal dialects, including Dendi, intensity is a redundant 'auxiliary feature' riding on the high tone (with a preference for the word-initial syllable and for closed syllables), not an independent word-stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. The only accent remarks for the tonal dialects are the auxiliary-feature statements (thesis p. 288 = SAL p. 279, formulated for Kaado and declared 'également valable pour les autres systèmes intonés'): 'le ton haut était lié à un accent d'intensité; l'intensité marquait de façon préférentielle l'initiale du mot; une syllabe fermée retenait plus l'accent qu'une syllabe ouverte', and (SAL p. 280) the redundant characters delimiting the accentual unit are 'accent sur l'initiale, accent sur la dernière syllabe haute, tension'.
new_statements.exceptions: Tersis 1968 reports three tones for the Gaya (Niger) Dendi (fn. 57 / fn. 12); Nicolaï elsewhere (thesis p. 34 fn. 35) wonders whether the Karimama/Gaya parler should count as Dendi or Zarma. Zarma differs from Dendi by tonal-contrast rules in combination (tone raising, contraction). Complex (rising/falling) tones never occur on a short open interior syllable nor interior in a trisyllable (SAL p. 282); the definite morpheme surfaces as a final rising tone; final rising tones otherwise only in rare loans (SAL pp. 285-286).
new_statements.domain_note: Word (lexical 'unité élémentaire', typically di-/trisyllabic) tone patterns in citation forms and in combination; at phrase level the strongest intensity marks the initial group and downdrift operates (SAL p. 280). The accent statements are typological/comparative generalizations over the tonal dialects, made explicitly for Kaado and extended to the other tonal systems; they are not a Dendi-specific stress rule. Dendi data are Nicolaï's own (parlers of Djougou, Parakou, Kandi; cf. Nicolaï 1978 'Les parlers dendi').
new_statements.identity_note: Nicolaï's 'dendi' = the parlers of Djougou, Parakou and Kandi in northern Benin (thesis abbreviations p. V; SAL 1982 p. 313), i.e. dend1243 proper (Glottolog lgcode for Nicolaï 1978: 'Mainly Kandi'). The Gaya/Malanville (Niger) variety described by Tersis 1968 is reported with three tones and Nicolaï (thesis p. 34 fn. 35) doubts whether it is Dendi or Zarma (zarm1239); Zima 1994 describes Djougou Dendi; Zima 1976 concerns the Salaga (Ghana) Dendi enclave. The statement is a typological classification (four-tone system, no stress system) from a comparative thesis, verified on the page image, not a dedicated Dendi grammar.

new_statements.quote: Type 4: Système tonal permettant quatre distinctions dans le cadre syllabique {CV́, CV̀, CV̌, CV̂}. Il peut dans la plupart des cas se réduire à une opposition entre deux valeurs tonales par le biais d'une analyse en mores [Nicolaï 1976, Tersis 1972a]. Les combinaisons des tons à l'intérieur des polysyllabes sont déterminées par des règles, de même que les combinaisons des unités entre elles. Ce système est réalisé en zarma et en dendi¹² qui ne se distinguent l'un de l'autre que par l'existence en zarma de quelques règles portant sur les contrastes dans le cadre des unités en combinaison [Tersis 1972a]. — fn. 12: Toutefois N. Tersis dit que le dendi de Gaya a trois tons; cf. N. Tersis [1972b:3-4].
new_statements.translation: Type 4: a tonal system allowing four distinctions within the syllable {CV́, CV̀, CV̌, CV̂}. In most cases it can be reduced to an opposition between two tonal values by means of a moraic analysis [Nicolaï 1976, Tersis 1972a]. Tone combinations inside polysyllables are governed by rules, as are combinations of units with one another. This system is realised in Zarma and in Dendi, which differ from each other only in that Zarma has a few rules bearing on contrasts between units in combination [Tersis 1972a]. — fn. 12: However, N. Tersis says that the Dendi of Gaya has three tones; cf. Tersis [1972b: 3-4].
new_statements.citation: Nicolaï, Robert (1982). Problèmes de dynamique linguistique: recherches en prosodie songhay. Studies in African Linguistics 13(3): 273-322.
new_statements.locator: p. 281 (typology, Type 4 and footnote 12); also p. 273 abstract, p. 282 §5, p. 291 §9, p. 313 dialect list
new_statements.reading: Dendi (Djougou, Parakou, Kandi) is a tone language with four syllabic tone distinctions (high, low, rising, falling), analysable as H/L on moras, i.e. the same system as Zarma; the accentual systems (fixed accent on the last long or final syllable in Western Songhay; limited or free accent in Eastern and Northern Songhay) belong to other Songhay dialects. No word stress is described for Dendi. The Niger (Gaya) variety is reported by Tersis as three-toned. For a stress catalog this codes as a tone language without lexical stress.
